claim: Rhabdomeric opsins (r-opsins) are light sensors in cephalic eye photoreceptors.
source: Rhabdomeric opsins (r-opsins) are light sensors in cephalic eye photoreceptors, but also function in additional sensory organs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about r-opsins.

claim: Rhabdomeric opsins function in additional sensory organs beyond cephalic eye photoreceptors.
source: Rhabdomeric opsins (r-opsins) are light sensors in cephalic eye photoreceptors, but also function in additional sensory organs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: Non-cephalic r-opsin1-expressing cells possess a full set of phototransduction components.
source: Non-cephalic cells possess a full set of phototransduction components, but also a mechanosensory signature.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomic profiling data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Non-cephalic r-opsin1-expressing cells possess a mechanosensory signature.
source: Non-cephalic cells possess a full set of phototransduction components, but also a mechanosensory signature.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomic profiling and statistical analyses presented in Figure 3.

claim: nompc and pkd2.1 co-express with r-opsin1 in TRE cells.
source: Prompted by the latter, we investigated Platynereis putative mechanotransducer and found that nompc and pkd2.1 co-expressed with r-opsin1 in TRE cells by HCR RNA-FISH.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by HCR RNA-FISH experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: r-Opsin1 is a Gαq-coupled blue light receptor.
source: To further assess the role of r-Opsin1 in these cells, we studied its signaling properties and unraveled that r-Opsin1 is a Gαq-coupled blue light receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by bioluminescence assays and spectral sensitivity measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: In non-cephalic cells, light mediated by r-Opsin1 adjusts the expression level of a calcium transporter relevant for auditory mechanosensation in vertebrates.
source: Profiling of cells from r-opsin1 mutants versus wild-types, and a comparison under different light conditions reveals that in the non-cephalic cells light – mediated by r-Opsin1 – adjusts the expression level of a calcium transporter relevant for auditory mechanosensation in vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomic profiling data comparing mutant vs. wild-type and different light conditions shown in Figure 6A and 6D.

claim: There is a light- and r-Opsin-1-dependent fine-tuning of the worm's undulatory movements in headless trunks.
source: We establish a deep-learning-based quantitative behavioral analysis for animal trunk movements and identify a light– and r-Opsin-1–dependent fine-tuning of the worm's undulatory movements in headless trunks, which are known to require mechanosensory feedback.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: Undulatory movements in headless trunks require mechanosensory feedback.
source: We establish a deep-learning-based quantitative behavioral analysis for animal trunk movements and identify a light– and r-Opsin-1–dependent fine-tuning of the worm's undulatory movements in headless trunks, which are known to require mechanosensory feedback.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: A multisensory cell type evolved to allow for fine-tuning of mechanosensation by light.
source: These results point towards a concept in which such a multisensory cell type evolved to allow for fine-tuning of mechanosensation by light.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results presented in the abstract, based on the data collected.

claim: Light-independent mechanosensory roles of r-opsins may have evolved secondarily.
source: This implies that light-independent mechanosensory roles of r-opsins may have evolved secondarily.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the results in the abstract.

claim: Rhabdomeric opsins are an ancient class of opsins particularly widespread among invertebrates.
source: Rhabdomeric opsins (r-opsins) are an ancient class of opsins particularly widespread among invertebrates, typically expressed in larval photoreceptor cells and cephalic eyes that rely on rhabdomeric photoreceptors (Arendt et al., 2002; Arendt and Wittbrodt, 2001; Ramirez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Rhabdomeric opsins are typically expressed in larval photoreceptor cells and cephalic eyes that rely on rhabdomeric photoreceptors.
source: Rhabdomeric opsins (r-opsins) are an ancient class of opsins particularly widespread among invertebrates, typically expressed in larval photoreceptor cells and cephalic eyes that rely on rhabdomeric photoreceptors (Arendt et al., 2002; Arendt and Wittbrodt, 2001; Ramirez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The role of r-opsins in light perception has been best studied in the model of the Drosophila eye photoreceptor (EP) cells.
source: The role of r-opsins in light perception has been best studied in the model of the Drosophila eye photoreceptor (EP) cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Stimulation of a light-sensitive chromophore (retinaldehyde) covalently bound to the Gαq-coupled r-opsin apoprotein initiates an intracellular cascade that leads to an increase in intracellular calcium.
source: Stimulation of a light-sensitive chromophore (retinaldehyde) covalently bound to the Gαq-coupled r-opsin apoprotein initiates an intracellular cascade (with 12 key components of the phototransduction cascade) that leads to an increase in intracellular calcium (reviewed in Hardie and Juusola, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The r-opsin phototransduction cascade has 12 key components.
source: Stimulation of a light-sensitive chromophore (retinaldehyde) covalently bound to the Gαq-coupled r-opsin apoprotein initiates an intracellular cascade (with 12 key components of the phototransduction cascade) that leads to an increase in intracellular calcium (reviewed in Hardie and Juusola, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Non-cephalic r-opsin-expressing cells are found in representatives of various animal groups.
source: Whereas most of our knowledge about the function of r-opsins in animal photoreception stems from studies on cephalic EPs, non-cephalic r-opsin-expressing cells are found in representatives of various animal groups.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: r-opsin homologs demarcate putative photoreceptor cells at the tube feet of sea urchins.
source: For instance, r-opsin homologs demarcate putative photoreceptor cells at the tube feet of sea urchins (Raible et al., 2006; Ullrich-Luter et al., 2011), and in Joseph cells and photoreceptors of the dorsal ocelli of the basal chordate amphioxus (Koyanagi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: r-opsin homologs are found in Joseph cells and photoreceptors of the dorsal ocelli of the basal chordate amphioxus.
source: For instance, r-opsin homologs demarcate putative photoreceptor cells at the tube feet of sea urchins (Raible et al., 2006; Ullrich-Luter et al., 2011), and in Joseph cells and photoreceptors of the dorsal ocelli of the basal chordate amphioxus (Koyanagi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Non-cephalic photoreceptor cells in the brittle star have been implicated in a form of vision.
source: In the case of the brittle star, such non-cephalic photoreceptor cells have been implicated in a form of vision (Sumner-Rooney et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: r-opsin genes are expressed in certain classes of mechanosensory cell types, such as the Johnston organ (JO) neurons and the larval Chordotonal organ (ChO) of Drosophila.
source: However, r-opsin genes have also started to be implied in functions that are unrelated to photoreception. Most notably, r-opsin genes are expressed in certain classes of mechanosensory cell types, such as the Johnston organ (JO) neurons and the larval Chordotonal organ (ChO) of Drosophila (Senthilan et al., 2012; Zanini et al., 2018), or the neuromasts of the lateral line of zebrafish and frog (Backfisch et al., 2013; Baker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: r-opsin genes are expressed in the neuromasts of the lateral line of zebrafish and frog.
source: However, r-opsin genes have also started to be implied in functions that are unrelated to photoreception. Most notably, r-opsin genes are expressed in certain classes of mechanosensory cell types, such as the Johnston organ (JO) neurons and the larval Chordotonal organ (ChO) of Drosophila (Senthilan et al., 2012; Zanini et al., 2018), or the neuromasts of the lateral line of zebrafish and frog (Backfisch et al., 2013; Baker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Several r-opsins expressed in JO and ChO neurons are required for proper mechanosensation.
source: Experiments assessing functionality of mechanosensation in both JO and ChO neurons have revealed that several r-opsins expressed in these receptors are required for proper mechanosensation and suggest that this function is light-independent (Senthilan et al., 2012; Zanini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The mechanosensory function of r-opsins in JO and ChO neurons is light-independent.
source: Experiments assessing functionality of mechanosensation in both JO and ChO neurons have revealed that several r-opsins expressed in these receptors are required for proper mechanosensation and suggest that this function is light-independent (Senthilan et al., 2012; Zanini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A subset of mechanosensory cells exhibit significant similarities in their molecular specification cascade with EPs, comprising analogous use of Pax, Atonal, or Pou4f3 transcription factors.
source: These functional findings add new perspectives to older observations that a subset of mechanosensory cells (to which JO and ChO cells belong) exhibit significant similarities in their molecular specification cascade with EPs, comprising analogous use of Pax, Atonal, or Pou4f3 transcription factors (Fritzsch, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The Platynereis r-opsin1 gene is expressed in EPs and in peripheral cells along the trunk of the animal (TRE cells).
source: The Platynereis r-opsin1 gene is not only expressed in EPs (Arendt et al., 2002), but also in peripheral cells along the trunk of the animal (Backfisch et al., 2013) (cells referred to in this study as trunk r-opsin1 expressing [TRE] cells), making the worm an attractive species for a comparative assessment of r-opsin function between cephalic and non-cephalic cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Both EP and TRE cells express the gaq gene that encodes a Gαq subunit.
source: While both EP and TRE cells express the gaq gene that encodes a Gαq subunit (Backfisch et al., 2013), it has remained elusive whether the TRE cells represent a segmental repetition of the EP cell type along the body plan or represent a distinct sensory modality.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: 278 genes are significantly enriched in EP cells.
source: From a total of 39,575 genes, we determined a set of 278 genes (0.7%) to be significantly enriched in EP cells and a set of 361 genes (0.9%) significantly enriched in TRE cells (False Discovery Rate [FDR] < 0.05) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 361 genes are significantly enriched in TRE cells.
source: From a total of 39,575 genes, we determined a set of 278 genes (0.7%) to be significantly enriched in EP cells and a set of 361 genes (0.9%) significantly enriched in TRE cells (False Discovery Rate [FDR] < 0.05) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 133 genes are shared between the EP and TRE cells (common EP-/TRE-enriched genes).
source: 133 genes (0.3% of total) were shared between the EP and TRE cells (common EP-/TRE-enriched genes), including, expectedly, r-opsin1 and gq (Supplementary file 1), and leaving 145 (0.4% of total) EP-specific genes and 228 (0.6% of total) TRE-specific genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: r-opsin1 and gq are among the common EP-/TRE-enriched genes.
source: 133 genes (0.3% of total) were shared between the EP and TRE cells (common EP-/TRE-enriched genes), including, expectedly, r-opsin1 and gq (Supplementary file 1), and leaving 145 (0.4% of total) EP-specific genes and 228 (0.6% of total) TRE-specific genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: 145 genes are EP-specific.
source: 133 genes (0.3% of total) were shared between the EP and TRE cells (common EP-/TRE-enriched genes), including, expectedly, r-opsin1 and gq (Supplementary file 1), and leaving 145 (0.4% of total) EP-specific genes and 228 (0.6% of total) TRE-specific genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 228 genes are TRE-specific.
source: 133 genes (0.3% of total) were shared between the EP and TRE cells (common EP-/TRE-enriched genes), including, expectedly, r-opsin1 and gq (Supplementary file 1), and leaving 145 (0.4% of total) EP-specific genes and 228 (0.6% of total) TRE-specific genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Putative homologs of 9 of the 12 key components of the r-opsin phototransduction pathway are enriched in the P. dumerilii EP cells.
source: By extending our assessment to bona fide homologs of additional components of the Drosophila r-opsin phototransduction pathway, we found that putative homologs of 9 and 8 of the 12 key components of the r-opsin phototransduction pathway are enriched in the P. dumerilii EP and TRE cells, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Putative homologs of 8 of the 12 key components of the r-opsin phototransduction pathway are enriched in the P. dumerilii TRE cells.
source: By extending our assessment to bona fide homologs of additional components of the Drosophila r-opsin phototransduction pathway, we found that putative homologs of 9 and 8 of the 12 key components of the r-opsin phototransduction pathway are enriched in the P. dumerilii EP and TRE cells, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The enrichment of phototransduction pathway components in EP cells is highly significant (p<10−4).
source: Statistical analysis with 104 random gene sets of matching size (see Materials and methods) revealed these results to be highly significant (p<10−4, for both EP and TRE).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on statistical analysis.

claim: The enrichment of phototransduction pathway components in TRE cells is highly significant (p<10−4).
source: Statistical analysis with 104 random gene sets of matching size (see Materials and methods) revealed these results to be highly significant (p<10−4, for both EP and TRE).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on statistical analysis.

claim: All 12 key components of the r-opsin phototransduction pathway are expressed in the TRE cells of P. dumerilii.
source: Of note, all 12 key components of the r-opsin phototransduction pathway were found to be expressed in the TRE cells of P. dumerilii (Figure 2B, C; p<10−4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Nine genes from the common EP-/TRE-enriched signature overlap with Drosophila JO neuron-specific genes.
source: Significant subsets of these were found in the common EP-/TRE-enriched signature (nine genes; p<10−4), and the TRE-specific signature (seven genes; p=1.3 × 10−3) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The overlap of nine genes between common EP-/TRE-enriched signature and Drosophila JO neuron-specific genes is highly significant (p<10−4).
source: Significant subsets of these were found in the common EP-/TRE-enriched signature (nine genes; p<10−4), and the TRE-specific signature (seven genes; p=1.3 × 10−3) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on statistical analysis.

claim: Seven genes from the TRE-specific signature overlap with Drosophila JO neuron-specific genes.
source: Significant subsets of these were found in the common EP-/TRE-enriched signature (nine genes; p<10−4), and the TRE-specific signature (seven genes; p=1.3 × 10−3) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The overlap of seven genes between TRE-specific signature and Drosophila JO neuron-specific genes is significant (p=1.3 × 10−3).
source: Significant subsets of these were found in the common EP-/TRE-enriched signature (nine genes; p<10−4), and the TRE-specific signature (seven genes; p=1.3 × 10−3) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on statistical analysis.

claim: The common EP-/TRE-enriched genes that overlap with JO neuron-specific genes essentially reflect P. dumerilii homologs of the phototransduction pathway.
source: The common EP-/TRE-enriched genes essentially reflect the P. dumerilii homologs of the aforementioned phototransduction pathway (rh3/rh4, rh5/rh6, trp/trpl, norpa, gβ76c, pip5k59b, arr2, and klp68D; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Bona fide homologs of mouse genes assigned to the GO category 'sensory perception of mechanical stimulus' are significantly overrepresented in the TRE-specific signature (p=0.029).
source: Indeed, these bona fide homologs are significantly overrepresented in the TRE-specific signature (p=0.029; Figure 3G, for gene IDs, see Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: 18 out of the 19 TRE-specific gene homologs have reported effects on hearing function in the mouse.
source: A closer analysis of those mouse mechanosensory genes whose bristleworm counterparts are expressed in TRE cells (Figure 3—source data 2) points at a gene signature shared between TRE cells and mouse inner ear hair (IEH) cells: 18 out of the 19 TRE-specific gene homologs have reported effects on hearing function in the mouse (yellow shading in Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on analysis of gene functions.

claim: There is a statistically significant overlap between mouse hearing genes and P. dumerilii TRE-specific genes (p=0.0087).
source: Again, we assessed the specificity of this finding by systematically comparing the overlap with mouse genes involved in distinct modalities of mechanosensation, confirming a statistically significant overlap between mouse hearing genes and P. dumerilii TRE-specific genes (p=0.0087; Figure 3J), whereas other mechanosensory modalities yielded no statistically significant results (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3J.

claim: P. dumerilii r-Opsin1 activates Gαq signaling upon light exposure.
source: P. dumerilii r-opsin1-transfected HEK293 cells exhibited a significant response to light exposure, similar to the human melanopsin (positive control) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A based on cell culture assays.

claim: P. dumerilii r-Opsin1 does not activate Gαs signaling.
source: By contrast, using corresponding assays for Gαs or Gαi/o activation (Bailes et al., 2012; Bailes and Lucas, 2013), we detected no activation of either Gαs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or Gαi/o (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) by P. dumerilii r-Opsin1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A based on cell culture assays.

claim: P. dumerilii r-Opsin1 does not activate Gαi/o signaling.
source: By contrast, using corresponding assays for Gαs or Gαi/o activation (Bailes et al., 2012; Bailes and Lucas, 2013), we detected no activation of either Gαs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or Gαi/o (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) by P. dumerilii r-Opsin1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B based on cell culture assays.

claim: P. dumerilii r-Opsin1 specifically activates Gαq, similar to Drosophila r-opsins.
source: This indicates that Platynereis r-Opsin1 specifically activates Gαq, similar to Drosophila r-opsins.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the cell culture assay data.

claim: P. dumerilii r-Opsin1 has a λmax of 471 nm.
source: The optimal λmax for the template was determined by least squares as 471 nm (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B and 5C based on spectral sensitivity measurements.

claim: P. dumerilii r-Opsin1 maximally absorbs light in the blue range.
source: P. dumerilii r-Opsin1 therefore maximally absorbs light in the blue range, similar to other r-opsin orthologs, such as human melanopsin, which exhibits a λmax of around 480 nm (Bailes and Lucas, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on spectral sensitivity measurements.

claim: Human melanopsin exhibits a λmax of around 480 nm.
source: P. dumerilii r-Opsin1 therefore maximally absorbs light in the blue range, similar to other r-opsin orthologs, such as human melanopsin, which exhibits a λmax of around 480 nm (Bailes and Lucas, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: atp2b/c7424 is significantly depleted in mutant TRE cells compared to wild-type cells (FDR = 0.010).
source: By contrast, one gene (atp2b/c7424, P. dumerilii homolog of mouse atp2b2; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, red arrowhead) was significantly depleted in mutant TRE cells compared to wild-type cells (FDR = 0.010; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A based on transcriptomic profiling.

claim: atp2b/c7424 is a P. dumerilii homolog of mouse atp2b2.
source: By contrast, one gene (atp2b/c7424, P. dumerilii homolog of mouse atp2b2; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, red arrowhead) was significantly depleted in mutant TRE cells compared to wild-type cells (FDR = 0.010; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: None of the identified phototransduction components were changed in r-opsin1 mutant TRE cells.
source: The specificity of this regulation is further supported by the fact that none of the identified phototransduction components were changed.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on transcriptomic profiling.

claim: The atp2b2 gene encodes a plasma membrane calcium-transporting ATPase.
source: The atp2b2 gene encodes a plasma membrane calcium-transporting ATPase, which is expressed in the stereocilia of mechanosensory cells of the murine cochlea and vestibular system (Street et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: atp2b2 is expressed in the stereocilia of mechanosensory cells of the murine cochlea and vestibular system.
source: The atp2b2 gene encodes a plasma membrane calcium-transporting ATPase, which is expressed in the stereocilia of mechanosensory cells of the murine cochlea and vestibular system (Street et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Homozygous atp2b2 mutant mice show balance deficits and are deaf.
source: Homozygous atp2b2 mutant mice show balance deficits and are deaf, while heterozygous mutants show partial loss of auditory ability (Kozel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Heterozygous atp2b2 mutant mice show partial loss of auditory ability.
source: Homozygous atp2b2 mutant mice show balance deficits and are deaf, while heterozygous mutants show partial loss of auditory ability (Kozel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: In zebrafish, atp2b2 is highly enriched in the r-opsin-expressing mechanosensory neuromasts of the lateral line.
source: Furthermore, in zebrafish, atp2b2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, dark blue arrowhead) is highly enriched in the r-opsin-expressing mechanosensory neuromasts of the lateral line (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), consistent with a potential mechanosensory function of the gene in this organism.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B based on qPCR data.

claim: atp2b/c7424 is significantly downregulated in dim light conditions compared to bright light (p=0.02).
source: Statistical analysis showed that atp2b/c7424 is significantly downregulated in dim light conditions as compared to bright light (p=0.02; Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 6D), similar to the downregulation observed in mutant worms (p=0.02; Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6D based on transcriptomic profiling.

claim: Blue light levels modulate atp2b/c7424 expression levels in TRE cells.
source: These results indicate that blue light levels modulate atp2b/c7424 expression levels in TRE cells and suggest that the light-dependent modulation is majorly mediated by r-Opsin1.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on transcriptomic profiling under different light conditions.

claim: The light-dependent modulation of atp2b/c7424 is majorly mediated by r-Opsin1.
source: These results indicate that blue light levels modulate atp2b/c7424 expression levels in TRE cells and suggest that the light-dependent modulation is majorly mediated by r-Opsin1.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison of mutant and wild-type data.

claim: Trans-heterozygous r-opsin1Δ1/Δ17 individuals responded to focal bright light stimuli but exhibited a significantly reduced net distance when compared to wild-type animals (p=0.02).
source: Trans-heterozygous r-opsin1Δ1/Δ17 individuals clearly responded to such stimuli, but exhibited a significantly reduced net distance when compared to wild-type animals (p=0.02; Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 based on behavioral analysis.

claim: Wild-type worms exhibited a light-dependent modulation of undulatory movements, which were higher during darkness.
source: Analyses on a total of 64 trunks revealed that wild-type (black graphs) exhibited a light-dependent modulation of the undulatory movements, which were higher during darkness (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6F-H based on behavioral analysis.

claim: The light-dependent modulation of undulatory movements was abolished in r-ops1-/- worms.
source: This modulation was abolished in r-ops1-/- worms, whose trunks exhibited equally high undulatory movements during light and dark (Figure 6F–H, red graphs).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6F-H based on behavioral analysis.

claim: In TRE cells, r-Opsin1 mediates light-dependent modulation of mechanosensory functions.
source: These results hint that in TRE cells r-Opsin1 mediates light-dependent modulation of mechanosensory functions, thereby impacting on regular behavioral movements.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on behavioral and molecular data.

claim: TRE cells represent a distinct mechanoreceptive cell type in which r-Opsin1 elicits light-dependent functional changes.
source: Our data, therefore, suggest that TRE cells represent a distinct mechanoreceptive cell type, in which r-Opsin1, in difference to the current Drosophila-based paradigms, elicits light-dependent functional changes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on the data presented.

claim: Photo- and mechanosensory systems have a common evolutionary origin in a multimodal sensory cell type.
source: Our results are consistent with the idea that photo- and mechanosensory systems have a common evolutionary origin in a multimodal sensory cell type.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Opsin-induced, phospholipase C-mediated PIP2 cleavage results in a fast-propagating change in photoreceptor bilayer curvature that triggers stretch-sensitive TRP-C channels.
source: Specifically, this model proposes that opsin-induced, phospholipase C-mediated PIP2 cleavage results in a fast-propagating change in photoreceptor bilayer curvature that then triggers stretch-sensitive TRP-C channels.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to a model from Drosophila EP function.

claim: Photon absorption (light reception) is effectively translated into a local stretch signal in various mechanosensory cell types.
source: Thereby, photon absorption (light reception) is effectively translated into a local stretch signal as it is at the core of various mechanosensory cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the photomechanical response model.

claim: The conservation of r-opsin expression along with the respective signaling machinery suggests that opsin activation in mechanoreceptive cells may acutely tune the membrane curvature and thus the ability of stretch receptors to be activated.
source: Given that this mechanism seems to account for a canonical photoreceptive function of r-opsin in EP cells, the conservation of r-opsin expression along with the respective signaling machinery suggests that opsin activation in mechanoreceptive cells may well acutely tune the membrane curvature and thus the ability of stretch receptors to be activated.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative interpretation.

claim: A light-modulatory function could effectively serve to adjust mechanosensory functions in species exposed to varying light conditions.
source: From an ecological perspective, a light-modulatory function could effectively serve to adjust mechanosensory functions in species exposed to varying light conditions, allowing them to tune mechanoreceptive responses to ambient light.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative interpretation.

claim: The absence of apparent light sensitivity in Drosophila JO or ChO neurons likely represents secondary evolutionary processes rather than ancestral conditions.
source: From this perspective, the absence of apparent light sensitivity in Drosophila JO or ChO neurons likely represents secondary evolutionary processes rather than ancestral conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative interpretation.

claim: The pMos{rops::egfp}vbci2 strain expresses enhanced GFP (EGFP) under the regulatory control of the Platynereis r-opsin1 gene in both EP and TRE cells.
source: Here, we established a dissociation and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) protocol for the Platynereis pMos{rops::egfp}vbci2 strain that expresses enhanced GFP (EGFP) under the regulatory control of the Platynereis r-opsin1 gene in both EP and TRE cells (Backfisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Both r-opsin1 and egfp were up to several thousand times more abundant in libraries derived from EGFP-positive cells than in those of unsorted cells.
source: Both r-opsin1 and egfp were up to several thousand times more abundant in libraries derived from EGFP-positive cells than in those of unsorted cells (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Gq was strongly expressed in EP and TRE cells.
source: Gq was previously shown to be strongly expressed in EP and TRE cells (Backfisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Signatures of EGFP-positive cells were consistently enriched in the gq gene encoding the G alpha subunit Gαq.

claim: The genes encoding the ribosomal subunit Rps9 or the Polo-like Kinase Cdc5 were not enriched in either EP or TRE cell populations.
source: By contrast, the genes encoding the ribosomal subunit Rps9 or the Polo-like Kinase Cdc5, previously established as internal controls for gene expression quantification experiments (Zantke et al., 2013), were not enriched in either EP or TRE cell populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: r-opsin3 has been described to be expressed in TREs.
source: While r-opsin3 has already been described to be expressed in TREs (Randel et al., 2013), also Go-opsin1and l-cry were part of the specific TRE transcriptome, pointing at an unexpected complexity of light receptors in the TRE cells, and a similar equipment of EP and TRE cells with photoreceptive molecules.

claim: The EP-derived transcriptome was enriched in the circadian clock gene bmal.
source: In line with these expectations, we found the EP-, but not TRE-derived transcriptomes to be enriched, respectively, in the circadian clock gene bmal, as well as a homolog of the embryonic lethal, abnormal vision/elav gene, a marker characteristic for committed neurons (Denes et al., 2007; Kerner et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on transcriptomic profiling.

claim: The number of common EP-/TRE-enriched genes significantly exceeds random expectation (p=0.024).

evidence: This is stated in the results based on statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pkd2.1 functions as a mechanical transducing molecule in Platynereis larvae.
source: Besides Pkd2.1 – previously shown to function as a mechanical transducing molecule in Platynereis larvae (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) – our analysis included Platynereis orthologs of the TRP-family member NOMPC (Pdu-NOMPC; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the PIEZO-family (Pdu-Piezo; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and of the TMC-family (Pdu-TMC1/2/3; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: NOMPC has been functionally validated as a mechanotransducer in other species.
source: Given the functional validation of Pkd2.1 as a mechanoreceptive molecule in Platynereis larvae (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) and the functional validation of NOMPC in other species (Fritzsch et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2000), our data further support the notion that TRE cells are indeed functional mechanoreceptors.
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.
